AB-410: Building Intelligent Applications — How Microsoft's New AI-First Builder Exam Replaced PL-200

📅 Nov 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

The AB-410 exam earns the Microsoft Certified: Intelligent Applications Builder Associate certification, and it tests whether a Power Platform builder can design Dataverse data models, build model-driven and canvas apps, automate business logic with cloud flows, and wire AI Hub prompts, models, and Copilot Studio agents into real business solutions. This article explains the AB-410 exam format, its three domains and weights, the 700 passing score, the AI-first topics it adds over the retired PL-200, and a practical six-week study plan for working builders.

Microsoft announced the AB-410 beta on May 27, 2026, and the exam reached general availability at the end of July 2026. The PL-200 exam it replaces retired on August 31, 2026, and a PL-200 certification already held stays on the holder's Microsoft Learn transcript but cannot be renewed. That timeline matters for anyone still studying from PL-200 material: the old exam's core of Dataverse, model-driven apps, canvas apps, and cloud flows survives, but AB-410 tests it through an AI-first lens, and the newest fifth of the exam — AI Hub prompts and models, prompt columns, generative pages, and agents created from canvas apps — has no PL-200 equivalent at all.

The shift is not cosmetic. In the PL-200 era, a functional consultant proved they could model data, build an app, and automate a process. In the AB-410 era, the same builder is expected to decide when a Copilot Studio agent belongs in the solution, when a prompt column is the right way to surface AI-generated content in a table, and when a business process flow should hand off to an agent instead of a human approver. Microsoft's own audience profile for the exam says candidates build AI-powered solutions using Copilot, agents, natural language prompts, and low-code tools, and that they collaborate with governance teams on responsible AI principles. If your Power Platform experience predates AI Hub, this exam will expose that gap quickly — which is exactly why this article spends so much of its length there.

The AB-410 exam is a 120-minute Pearson VUE test with a 700 passing score, and the exam earns the Microsoft Certified: Intelligent Applications Builder Associate credential.

Three details in that table deserve emphasis before you plan anything else. First, Microsoft has not published a question count for AB-410, so any source quoting an exact number is guessing; the honest figure is the 40–60 range Microsoft publishes for its certification portfolio. Second, the 120-minute duration is the majority figure across prep sources and matches what the certification page states, but one established prep guide still lists approximately 100 minutes — the conflict is recorded in full later in this article. Third, the credential is valid for only twelve months, and the free renewal assessment opens six months before expiry, so AB-410 is a certification you maintain, not one you earn once and forget.

The AB-410 exam replaced the PL-200 exam on August 31, 2026, because Microsoft needed a credential that tests AI-integrated Power Platform building rather than traditional low-code app development alone.

PL-200 was the Microsoft Power Platform Functional Consultant Associate exam, and for years it was the standard credential for the people who configured Dataverse, built model-driven and canvas apps, and wired up Power Automate flows for a business. It did that job well. But the platform it certified changed underneath it: Copilot arrived inside app design, AI Hub arrived with prompts and models that drop straight into flows and forms, and agents became something a business app builder was expected to reason about rather than something a data scientist built in a separate tool. A credential that never asked about any of that stopped describing the job.

Microsoft's answer was not to bolt an AI module onto PL-200. AB-410 is a genuinely new exam built around a different role: the intelligent applications builder. The audience profile in the official study guide describes a professional who creates apps, data models, and flows that connect to agents, AI models and prompts, and visualizations — and who works with environment and security administrators on policies, roles, identity, and authentication, and with governance teams on responsible AI, application lifecycle management, solutions, pipelines, and monitoring. That collaboration list is itself a signal: AB-410 expects you to operate inside a larger, more structured delivery team, not as a solo app builder.

The launch followed a fast schedule. The beta opened in April 2026, and Microsoft offered the first 300 people who took the beta exam on or before June 17, 2026 an 80% discount with the code AB410KBMaui. General availability followed at the end of July 2026, and by October 2026 the certification page no longer carried a beta label. PL-200 registration closed ahead of the August 31, 2026 retirement, and Microsoft's own retirement table names Microsoft Certified: Intelligent Applications Builder Associate as the related new credential. If you hold PL-200, nothing is taken away — but the renewal path is gone, and the market signal has moved.

One more consequence of that newness is worth stating plainly: third-party preparation for AB-410 is still thin. As of September 2026, prep providers noted that Microsoft's own practice assessment had not yet shipped, and one guide still lists it as unavailable while another reports it live on Microsoft's AI Skills Navigator. The exam is young enough that the official study guide remains the single most reliable source, and every claim in this article is checked against it first.

The AB-410 exam measures three domains, and the business application logic and automation domain carries 40–45% of the exam, so study time should follow those published weights.

Microsoft publishes the weights as ranges, not fixed percentages, and the ranges have not changed between the guide's earlier version and its December 18, 2026 version. The three domains are Create a foundation for intelligent applications at 25–30%, Create intelligent applications at 25–30%, and Build business application logic and automation at 40–45%. The arithmetic is the whole study strategy: the third domain alone is worth nearly as much as the other two combined. A study plan that spends equal time on all three domains is a plan that under-invests in almost half the exam.

The AB-410 foundation domain covers 25–30% of the exam, and the domain tests AI-enabled solution design, environment choices, application lifecycle management, and Dataverse data modeling.

This domain splits into two skill groups, and both are decision-heavy rather than click-heavy. The first group, designing Power Platform solutions by using AI-enabled tools, asks you to analyze a business requirement and identify the right components and implementation options — canvas app, model-driven app, Copilot Studio agent, Power Pages site, or some combination — to evaluate built-in agents for inclusion in the solution, to recommend extensibility options when out-of-the-box capability falls short, to recommend environment types, and to deploy a solution and application lifecycle management strategy. The exam is testing judgment here: given a scenario, which pieces fit together, and which do not.

The second group is building data models in Dataverse, and it is where the exam shows its AI-era focus most clearly in this domain. You need to create and edit tables in the data workspace, create and modify standard tables, configure table properties, create and modify columns, and configure table relationships. Then come the two skills that separate AB-410 from PL-200: configuring prompt columns, which embed AI-generated content directly into a table column, and configuring row summaries, which generate AI summaries of record data. You also need public views, main forms, and table-level security configuration.

The throughline is that "foundation" does not mean basic. It means the decisions everything else in the solution depends on — get the data model or the solution architecture wrong here, and no amount of clever automation downstream fixes it. Study this domain by building a real Dataverse model for a real business process, including at least one prompt column and one row summary, rather than by reading about tables.

The AB-410 intelligent applications domain covers 25–30% of the exam, and the domain tests model-driven apps, canvas apps, generative pages, and Copilot Studio agent integration.

This domain covers the actual app-building work, split across model-driven and canvas apps, and it is worth treating each as a genuinely distinct skill set rather than two flavors of the same thing. For model-driven apps, you need to create and configure forms and views, create generative pages using natural language — a skill that reflects how much of modern Power Apps development now starts with a natural-language prompt rather than a blank canvas — compose a model-driven app from its component parts, configure access to forms, views, and the app itself, and create and configure charts and dashboards.

For canvas apps, the exam goes well beyond connecting a data source and adding controls. Expect content on designing apps for accessibility, performance, responsiveness, and usability — all four together, not just visual polish. You need to automate business processes directly from a canvas app, build reusable components including named formulas, user-defined functions, and component libraries, manage variables and collections correctly, implement proper error handling rather than letting a flow fail silently, and test canvas apps using Monitor to diagnose real runtime issues. One skill that specifically reflects the intelligent-applications framing of this exam is creating a Copilot Studio agent directly from a canvas app, a genuinely new workflow most PL-200-era candidates never had to learn.

The practical difference between the two app types is the exam's favorite trap. Model-driven apps are metadata-driven and Dataverse-centric: forms, views, and security roles do the work. Canvas apps are formula-driven and pixel-controlled: Power Fx, variables, collections, and components do the work. Scenario questions will present a requirement and ask which app type fits, or will describe a model-driven feature and ask how its canvas equivalent behaves. Knowing both deeply, and knowing where each stops, is the whole domain.

The AB-410 business logic and automation domain carries 40–45% of the exam, and the domain tests cloud flows, AI Hub prompts and models, business rules, and business process flows.

This is the domain that decides whether you pass, simply because of its sheer weight, and it covers three distinct technical areas that all deserve serious study time. The first is cloud flows: recommending the right trigger for a given scenario, evaluating and choosing appropriate connectors, managing approval processes through flows, configuring flow actions correctly, implementing control logic with conditions and loops, and — critically — testing and troubleshooting cloud flows when they do not behave as expected. That last skill is where a lot of real-world Power Automate work actually happens, and it is tested accordingly.

The second area is prompts and models in AI Hub, the most distinctly current content on the entire exam. You need to build a prompt from a template or from blank, consume that prompt inside both apps and cloud flows, add knowledge sources to ground a prompt's responses, customize prompt settings including which underlying model it uses, add structured inputs so a prompt can be parameterized rather than static, and consume a standalone AI model — not just a prompt — inside both apps and flows. If your prior Power Platform experience predates AI Hub, this is very likely your single biggest study gap, and it deserves dedicated hands-on time rather than passive reading.

The third area is business and process logic: configuring business rules and business process flows — both long-standing Power Platform capabilities that remain fully relevant — alongside calculated, rollup, and formula columns, and evaluating which use cases call for which kind of business logic. This is the domain where experienced functional consultants coming from PL-200-era knowledge will feel most at home, but it is worth resisting the temptation to skim it just because it feels familiar, since the exam still expects precision on when each logic type is the right tool.

The AB-410 exam tests AI Hub prompts and models as a skill, and the exam expects candidates to build prompts, add knowledge sources, and consume prompts inside apps and flows.

AI Hub is the single largest new surface in AB-410, and it is the area where PL-200 study material helps least. Start with the vocabulary, because the exam uses it precisely. A prompt is a reusable instruction you build from a template or from blank, with structured inputs that let it accept parameters instead of fixed text. A model is a standalone AI model you consume directly — for text generation, classification, extraction, or similar tasks — without wrapping it in a prompt first. Knowledge is the grounding material you attach to a prompt so its responses draw on your business data rather than on general training. Prompt settings include which underlying model the prompt runs on, and changing the model changes the behavior, cost, and output quality.

The exam tests the full lifecycle, not just the definitions. You build the prompt, you add knowledge to it, you customize its settings, and then you consume it — in a canvas app, in a model-driven app, and in a cloud flow — and you do the same for a standalone model. Scenario questions will ask where a prompt belongs: in the app that shows the result to the user, or in the flow that processes the record in the background. They will ask what happens when a prompt has no knowledge source attached, and what changes when you add one. They will ask which model setting to change when the output is wrong in a specific way.

The study method that works here is building, not reading. Create a prompt from a template, then rebuild the same prompt from blank. Add a knowledge source and test the same question with and without it, so you can see grounding change the answer. Consume the prompt in a canvas app control and then in a cloud flow action, and note how the inputs and outputs differ between the two surfaces. Then consume a standalone model in both places and note what a model gives you that a prompt does not. Two focused afternoons of this will teach you more about the AI Hub skills than a week of reading descriptions.

Responsible AI belongs in this section too, because the exam ties it to the same features. Building a solution that calls an AI Hub prompt or model, or that hands off to a Copilot Studio agent, introduces governance questions a traditional canvas-app-plus-Dataverse solution never raised: what data is the model grounded on, who can configure or modify a prompt's knowledge sources, and how is AI-generated content in a prompt column or row summary reviewed before it is trusted. The exam does not expect you to be a governance specialist, but it does expect you to think about these questions when you design a solution, and the audience profile explicitly calls out collaboration with governance teams on responsible AI principles.

The AB-410 exam tests model-driven apps and canvas apps as distinct skills, and the exam expects candidates to choose the right app type for each business requirement.

The cleanest way to hold the distinction is to ask who controls the layout. In a model-driven app, Dataverse metadata controls the layout: tables, forms, views, and security roles define what the user sees, and the app is assembled from those components. In a canvas app, you control the layout: every control is placed by hand, every behavior is written in Power Fx, and responsiveness, accessibility, and performance are your design decisions rather than platform defaults. The exam tests whether you know which model fits a given requirement, and the wrong choice in a scenario question is usually the app type that could technically do the job but fights the requirement.

Model-driven apps fit requirements that are data-shaped: a team working through records in a table, with forms for detail, views for lists, charts and dashboards for oversight, and role-based access deciding who sees which form or view. Generative pages fit here too — the exam specifically lists creating generative pages using natural language as a model-driven skill, which means describing the page you want and letting the platform generate it. Canvas apps fit requirements that are experience-shaped: a custom interface for a specific task, a mobile-first form for field workers, a screen that automates a business process inline, or a reusable component library shared across several apps.

The canvas-app skills list is the more demanding of the two, and it rewards hands-on practice. Named formulas, user-defined functions, and component libraries are relatively advanced Power Fx capabilities, and the exam lists all three. Variables and collections must be managed correctly — knowing when state lives in a variable, when it lives in a collection, and when it should live in neither because Dataverse should hold it. Error handling must be implemented deliberately, so a failed flow or connector call surfaces a message instead of failing silently. And Monitor is the named testing tool: you test a canvas app by running it under Monitor and reading what actually happened at runtime, not by staring at the formula bar.

Study both app types by building the same small business process twice — once as a model-driven app and once as a canvas app — and writing down every point where the two builds diverge. That comparison is the exam in miniature.

The AB-410 exam tests Dataverse modeling in depth, and the exam expects candidates to distinguish calculated, rollup, and formula columns and to configure prompt columns and row summaries.

Dataverse is the foundation the whole exam stands on, and the questions here punish shallow knowledge more than anywhere else except the automation domain. The column-type distinction is the classic trap, and it is worth learning cold. A calculated column computes its value from other columns on the same record, in real time, using a formula — it is for values derived from the record itself. A rollup column aggregates values from related records — a sum, count, average, minimum, or maximum across a relationship — and it is computed on a schedule, not instantly. A formula column is the newer type: it uses Power Fx, it can reference columns across related tables, and it behaves like a calculated column with a more expressive language. Scenario questions will describe a requirement and ask which column type fits; the wrong answers will always be plausible, and the deciding detail will be whether the value comes from the same record, from related records, or needs Power Fx expressions.

Relationships and security are the other half of the foundation. You need to configure table relationships correctly — one-to-many, many-to-many, and the self-referential cases that trip people up — and to configure table-level security so the right roles see the right records. The exam also tests the newer AI-flavored table features in this context: prompt columns that embed AI-generated content into a table, and row summaries that generate AI summaries of record data. Know what each one produces, where its output appears, and what governs it — a prompt column's output depends on its prompt and its inputs, and a row summary depends on the record's data.

Environment types belong here too, since the exam lists recommending environment types as a foundation skill. Development, test, and production environments exist for a reason, and the exam will present scenarios where the wrong environment choice creates a governance or data problem. Pair that with the solution and application lifecycle management strategy the exam also lists: solutions package components for movement between environments, pipelines automate the promotion, and the whole structure exists so a change can be tested before it reaches production users. Study Dataverse by modeling a real process end to end — tables, relationships, the right column types, security roles, a prompt column, and a row summary — and then moving it through environments as a solution.

The AB-410 exam tests cloud flows and business logic across its heaviest domain, and the exam expects candidates to pick correct triggers, connectors, approvals, and control logic for each scenario.

Cloud flows reward the candidate who has actually debugged one. The exam's skill list reads like a working consultant's week: recommend the right trigger for a scenario, evaluate and recommend connectors, manage approvals through flows, configure flow actions, implement control logic with conditions and loops, and test and troubleshoot flows. The trigger question is the most common trap — an automated trigger, an instant trigger, and a scheduled trigger each fit different requirements, and a scenario that says "when a record is created" is pointing at a different trigger than one that says "every Monday at 9 a.m." or "when a user presses a button in the app." Connectors are the second trap: standard connectors, premium connectors, and custom connectors have different licensing and availability implications, and the exam expects you to notice which one a scenario requires.

Approvals deserve their own study pass. Managing an approval process through a cloud flow means knowing the approval types, what happens when an approver does not respond, and how the flow branches on approval versus rejection. Control logic is the same story: conditions and loops are simple to describe and easy to get wrong in a scenario, especially when a loop must process a collection of records and handle the failure of a single item without failing the whole run. And troubleshooting is explicitly listed as a skill, so practice reading a failed flow run, finding the action that failed, and explaining why — that diagnostic sequence is itself an exam skill.

Business rules and business process flows are the quieter half of this domain, and they are easy to under-study because they feel familiar. A business rule applies logic at the form level: show or hide a field, set a value, lock a field, based on conditions on the record. A business process flow guides a user through stages of a process, with steps and branching, and it is for processes where the path matters as much as the outcome. The exam's skill is evaluating use cases for business logic — knowing when a business rule fits, when a business process flow fits, when a cloud flow fits, and when a calculated, rollup, or formula column is the right tool instead. The four options will all appear in scenario questions, and the deciding detail will be where the logic runs and who experiences it.

The AB-410 study plan below spends six weeks across the three domains in proportion to their weights, and the plan pairs hands-on Power Platform practice with timed question practice weekly.

This plan assumes you already work in Power Platform at a functional-consultant level — you can build a canvas app, model a Dataverse table, and write a basic cloud flow. If Dataverse is new to you, add two weeks at the front for data modeling fundamentals. The plan totals roughly 8–10 hours a week, and every week ends with a timed practice set so the exam format becomes routine before test day.

Weeks 1 and 2 cover the foundation domain at 25–30%. Weeks 3 and 4 cover the intelligent applications domain at 25–30%. Weeks 5 and 6 cover the automation domain at 40–45% — two full weeks, because that domain is nearly half the exam and because its AI Hub half is the newest material for most candidates. If you have to cut the plan short, cut from weeks 1 and 2, never from weeks 5 and 6.

Each week, finish with a timed set of 20–30 practice questions mapped to that week's domain, and keep a running list of every question you miss with the reason you missed it. In the final three days before the exam, take one full timed run of 40–60 questions, review every miss, and re-read the official study guide's skills list one more time — any bullet you cannot explain from experience is a topic to revisit, because the guide's own note says related topics may be covered and any listed skill is fair game.

The AB-410 exam is booked through Microsoft Learn and delivered by Pearson VUE online or at a test center, and the exam costs 165 US dollars in the United States.

Booking starts on the Microsoft Learn certification page, which hands off to Pearson VUE for scheduling. You can sit the exam online with OnVUE proctoring from your home or office, or in person at a test center. The exam itself is 120 minutes, and the appointment runs to about 140 minutes including check-in. Microsoft's exam policy notes that the paper may include interactive components alongside standard multiple-choice items, and one prep guide reports that Microsoft Learn is open in a split screen throughout role-based exams — useful if true, but confirm it in the current exam policy before relying on it.

The passing score is 700 on Microsoft's 1,000-point scaled score, and Microsoft states outright that the scaled score may not equal 70% of the points — do not try to convert your practice percentage into a pass prediction. Microsoft does not publish the question count, and the published range for its certification portfolio is 40 to 60 questions, with the number varying by exam. Unscored trial items may appear, and guessing is not penalized in the way candidates sometimes fear — answer every question, and use the review time at the end for flagged items rather than leaving anything blank.

If you do not pass, the retake policy reported by prep sources is 24 hours after the first attempt, then 14 days between later attempts — confirm the current policy on Microsoft Learn, since retake rules change. The exam fee is USD 165 in the United States, priced by the country or region where the exam is taken, with local taxes possibly applying. If English is not your preferred language, Microsoft's study guide notes that you can request an additional 30 minutes to complete the exam, which is a meaningful accommodation for non-native English speakers given the scenario-heavy format.

The AB-410 exam has facts that Microsoft has not published or that prep sources report differently, and the exam facts below record each conflict for candidates to verify before booking.

This section exists because AB-410 is a new exam and the prep ecosystem has not converged yet. Every conflict below was found in sources fetched on November 27, 2026, and each one is stated rather than smoothed over.

Duration: 120 minutes versus 100 minutes. The majority of prep sources — including Training Camp, ExamPrise, A Guide to Cloud, CertCompanion, and Trainocate — list 120 minutes, and one guide states that the certification page itself gives 120 minutes. One established prep guide, D365 Training, lists approximately 100 minutes. The 120-minute figure is used in this article because it is the majority figure and the one tied to the certification page, but the 100-minute figure exists and a candidate who sees it should know it is a real published number, not a typo they imagined.

Languages: English only versus 13 languages. This is the sharpest disagreement. CertCompanion, D365 Training, and Udemy course listings state that the exam is currently offered in English only. Training Camp and Trainocate state 13 languages, and Trainocate lists them: English, Arabic (Saudi Arabia), Chinese (Simplified), Chinese (Traditional), French, German, Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese (Brazil), Russian, and Spanish. One guide's September 2026 check recorded an English-only language list on the certification page. The Microsoft Learn study guide itself says the English version is updated first and localized versions follow about eight weeks later, and that the available languages are listed in the Schedule Exam section of the exam details page. The only safe action is to check that Schedule Exam section when you book — do not assume either figure.

Question count: unpublished. Microsoft does not publish a fixed question count for AB-410. The portfolio range of 40–60 questions is the honest figure, and any source quoting an exact count for this exam is estimating. Plan your pacing on 40–60 questions in 120 minutes, which is roughly two to three minutes per question including review time.

Practice assessment: available versus not available. Training Camp reports that Microsoft's practice assessment for AB-410 is now available on AI Skills Navigator, with sign-in required. A Guide to Cloud lists the Microsoft practice assessment as not available yet. This is a fast-moving fact on a new exam; check AI Skills Navigator directly before test day rather than trusting either statement.

Skills guide version: December 18, 2026. The Microsoft Learn study guide fetched for this article is headed "Skills measured as of December 18, 2026," with a change log recording minor changes to the audience profile and the solution-design skill group and no change to the domain weights. Candidates should expect the guide to keep evolving and should re-check it in the week they book.

The AB-410 certification is one of thirteen associate-level prerequisites for the AB-100 expert exam, and the AB-410 credential is valid for twelve months with free renewal through an online assessment.

AB-410 is not a dead end, and that is deliberate. Microsoft's new AI Business Solutions track stacks: the associate-level exams, including AB-410, AB-210, and AB-400, feed into the expert-level AB-100, Microsoft Certified: Agentic AI Business Solutions Architect Expert. The prerequisite list for AB-100 names thirteen associate-level certifications, and AB-410 is one of them — along with AI-103, AI-300, AB-210, AB-620, AB-250, PL-400, MB-330, MB-230, MB-310, MB-500, MB-800, and MB-820. Passing AB-100 before earning the prerequisite still counts, so the order is flexible, but the intended path is clear: build with AB-410, then architect with AB-100.

The renewal mechanics are the same across Microsoft's role-based certifications. The credential is valid for twelve months, and the free renewal assessment is an unproctored online assessment on Microsoft Learn that opens in the six months before expiry. Because AB-410's skills measured are still being updated — the December 18, 2026 version is already the second version — renewal is genuinely useful here rather than a formality: it forces a refresh against the current outline.

For career purposes, AB-410 positions its holder as the builder who can move fluidly between a Dataverse table design, a business process flow, and an AI Hub prompt configuration without handing work between three different people. Consulting firms delivering Power Platform implementations are seeing client requests that explicitly ask for AI-integrated solution design, not just app development, and a current credential that explicitly covers that work is a fast way to build trust with a client who has no other way to verify the skill. Longer-term, the certification opens toward senior tracks such as Power Platform Solution Architect, AI-Enabled Business Applications Consultant, or Intelligent Automation Lead — roles where the question is not whether you can build one app, but how AI capabilities, automation, and traditional app development fit together across an organization's broader estate.

The AB-410 exam rewards candidates who practice against its published domains under timed conditions, and the AB-410 practice questions below map to all three official skill domains.

Do not book the exam until you have taken at least one full timed practice run and reviewed every question you missed. The study4pass AB-410 practice set is mapped to the official skills outline across all three domains, with 75 questions covering the foundation, intelligent applications, and automation domains in proportion to their published weights: https://study4pass.com/study-material/microsoft/ab-410

Use that run diagnostically. If your misses cluster in the automation domain, spend your remaining study time on cloud flows and AI Hub, not on the app-building material you already know. If your misses cluster on column types and Dataverse modeling, rebuild the data model rather than re-reading the definitions. And if the AI Hub questions are your weakest area, that is expected — it is the newest material on the exam for almost every candidate — but it is also the area where two afternoons of hands-on building close the gap fastest. Book the exam when a timed run feels routine, not when the calendar says you should be ready.

Author: Study4Pass. Facts verified November 27, 2026 against the Microsoft Learn AB-410 study guide, the Microsoft Tech Community launch announcement, and convergent prep guides (Training Camp, D365 Training, ExamPrise, A Guide to Cloud, CertCompanion, Trainocate). Exam format, pricing, and skills weighting are set solely by Microsoft and change over time — confirm current specifics on the official Microsoft Learn certification page before you register.

Databricks Lakebase Safekeeper, Pageserver, and LTAP Architecture

📅 Nov 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

This guide explains how Databricks Lakebase separates PostgreSQL compute from durable storage, how Safekeepers and Pageservers participate in write and read paths, how log sequence numbers support versioned page reconstruction and branching, and how Lakebase connects transactional data to lakehouse analytics.

The implementation exercises use Databricks Free Edition as a perpetual, no-cost, serverless-only learning environment. Free Edition is appropriate for learning PostgreSQL behavior, Lakebase concepts, synthetic transaction workloads, branches, Unity Catalog tables, and analytical queries. It is not a production database service-level environment.

Lakebase does not simply write PostgreSQL .tar data chunks to local compute disks. Its PostgreSQL compute layer is stateless with respect to durable database storage. Durable state is maintained by a distributed storage layer made up of Safekeepers, Pageservers, and cloud object storage.

Safekeepers replicate and persist PostgreSQL write-ahead log records before a transaction commit is acknowledged. Databricks documents quorum-based WAL replication across availability zones. The internal consensus and replication implementation should be described using the official term “quorum replication” unless a specific Databricks source explicitly identifies a Paxos or Raft implementation.

Pageservers ingest WAL, maintain versioned page history, reconstruct PostgreSQL pages at a requested log sequence number, and use cloud object storage as the durable storage foundation. Pageservers are not the same as an application-visible Delta Lake or Apache Iceberg table.

Lakebase LTAP can expose transactional changes to the lakehouse through managed capabilities such as Lakebase Change Data Feed. This is different from claiming that every PostgreSQL INSERT is synchronously converted into a Delta or Iceberg Parquet file before commit.

Operational and analytical workloads can use a unified storage and governance architecture, but “zero pipeline” does not mean zero processing, zero latency, or literal zero data movement. Managed services still capture changes, materialize analytical formats, track freshness, and handle schema evolution.

Absolute point-in-time synchronization between a front-office order book and a back-office risk calculation must not be assumed. Production systems require explicit snapshot identifiers, source commit positions, LSN watermarks, event-time controls, and measured freshness.

Create a Databricks Free Edition workspace.

lakebase_storage_architecture_free_nonprod

Create a notebook named 00_environment_check and run:

Traditional PostgreSQL combines the query process, buffer cache, WAL handling, and database data files around one host or tightly attached storage system.

Before acknowledging a commit, PostgreSQL writes the transaction's WAL record to durable storage. WAL provides a sequential recovery record and allows PostgreSQL to recover modified pages after a failure.

PostgreSQL also maintains relation data files that materialize the current state of table and index pages. A normal PostgreSQL page is commonly 8 KB.

The traditional architecture is operationally simple, but compute and storage scaling are coupled. Creating a full branch, read replica, or point-in-time copy can require substantial copying, replay, or storage provisioning.

Lakebase retains PostgreSQL transaction semantics while separating the compute and durable storage responsibilities.

The Lakebase compute node runs a PostgreSQL-compatible query engine.

The compute node is stateless with respect to authoritative durable database storage. It can cache pages in memory and maintain temporary local runtime state, but the durable database does not depend on one compute instance's local disk.

Stateless does not mean that a compute interruption is invisible to every application. Applications should use connection retry, idempotency, and transaction retry patterns appropriate to PostgreSQL.

When an application executes an INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE, PostgreSQL changes pages in memory and emits WAL records describing the changes.

Instead of relying on one compute node's local WAL disk as the durable authority, the compute node streams WAL to multiple Safekeeper nodes.

A Safekeeper is a specialized WAL persistence service. It receives WAL, persists it, participates in replication, tracks LSN progress, and acknowledges durable receipt.

Lakebase acknowledges a committed transaction only after the required storage durability condition is satisfied. Databricks describes this as writing to multiple locations across availability zones and recording committed transactions durably before acknowledging them.

Exact exposed metric names can vary. Use the documented Lakebase monitoring interfaces rather than assuming all internal LSN values are available to clients.

Do not design an application around a fixed number of Safekeepers. Databricks manages the storage topology and redundancy.

Pageservers receive or retrieve durable WAL and transform it into a page-version history suitable for scalable reads and long-term storage.

The storage model is log structured and non-overwriting. Historical versions are retained under the service's retention and branching model rather than updating one authoritative page file in place.

A page version is addressed by a database object and page identity together with an LSN.

The internal implementation is managed by Databricks. Users should not build direct dependencies on private layer-file formats, local index structures, or undocumented storage APIs.

Incoming page changes and WAL-derived records are first accumulated in memory and organized for persistent storage.

When internal thresholds are reached, the storage engine creates immutable layer files.

A delta layer represents changes over a defined key and LSN range.

An image layer contains complete page images at a particular historical boundary. Image layers reduce how many deltas must be replayed for a read.

Compaction merges or reorganizes historical layers so reads do not need to traverse an unbounded sequence of small deltas.

Layer files can be uploaded to managed cloud object storage such as Amazon S3, Azure Data Lake Storage, or Google Cloud Storage, depending on the Databricks cloud.

Cloud object storage is the durable foundation. Pageservers provide the indexed and cached serving layer used by compute.

The thresholds, compaction schedules, index structures, and file sizes are service internals. Do not hard-code an assumption such as “every 1 GB creates one layer” into an institutional design unless the current Databricks documentation provides that contract.

When a required page is not present in the compute node's buffer cache, the compute layer requests the page from storage for a specific LSN.

The Pageserver finds the newest image layer at or before the requested LSN.

It then locates the relevant delta records after the image LSN and no later than the requested LSN.

The Pageserver replays those changes in order and reconstructs a standard PostgreSQL page.

The reconstructed page is returned to the compute node and can be cached in the PostgreSQL buffer cache.

This model supports historical page versions and branch timelines without maintaining a full physical copy for every compute or branch.

Do not promise that every page reconstruction completes in a fixed number of milliseconds. Latency depends on cache state, layer lookup, delta depth, object-storage access, network conditions, page history, and service load.

Lakebase branches use copy-on-write storage metadata.

A new branch references an existing parent timeline at a selected point. The branch initially shares the parent's historical storage rather than copying every database page.

New writes create a separate branch history.

A branch is not a Git repository. “Git-style branching” is an analogy for fast, isolated, copy-on-write histories. Database branches do not automatically provide text merges, semantic conflict resolution, or an unrestricted merge-to-production operation.

The order, decision, and status update commit atomically. Either all become durable or the transaction rolls back.

The storage service's WAL durability path is internal. The application receives normal PostgreSQL transaction semantics.

A historical branch represents the database state reachable from its selected timeline point. Its availability depends on the service's retention and restore capabilities.

Do not claim unlimited retention. Institutional retention requires an explicit policy, supported retention settings, backups or archival controls, and periodic restore tests.

For a learning workflow, a target such as 30 seconds can be reasonable. For front-office risk or order control, use the dedicated production control system and define a much stricter, independently validated requirement.

The supported path is Lakebase transactional data made available through LTAP capabilities as governed analytical data.

This is more defensible than claiming absolute synchronization without evidence.

Do not compare an unbounded live PostgreSQL table against a Delta table at a different point in time and label every difference an error.

A front-office trading application needs transactionally consistent order state, deterministic controls, and low-latency point operations. Use PostgreSQL transactions and the approved execution infrastructure.

A desk-risk application needs current position and limit data with an explicit freshness watermark. It can combine the operational change feed with market data and risk factors in Delta.

A back-office application needs complete lifecycle history, booking, allocation, settlement, and reconciliation evidence. It can use the immutable change history and independent sources.

An AI application needs governed access, data minimization, source citations, and model logging. It should not receive unrestricted order or customer details.

All consumers can use Unity Catalog governance for analytical assets. PostgreSQL permissions and Lakebase roles still require separate design for operational objects.

Show both the order source watermark and the market-data observation time. A synchronized database architecture does not make two external sources share the same event time.

Grant analysts access to curated views rather than raw change records unless they need the full event history.

Grant data engineers permissions to manage integration tables but not to approve trading actions.

Grant auditors read-only access to change history, analysis watermarks, lineage, and reconciliation results.

Use service principals for Lakebase integrations and scheduled analytical jobs.

Do not place PostgreSQL passwords, application tokens, or cloud credentials in notebooks.

Apply row filters and column masks to sensitive analytical data where supported.

Monitor Lakebase compute status, connection pressure, transaction errors, query latency, branch usage, storage consumption, and integration status.

Monitor the analytical path for source freshness, ingestion lag, schema drift, failed materialization, small-file growth, and query performance.

Internal Safekeeper and Pageserver metrics may not all be customer exposed. Use supported Databricks monitoring surfaces and support procedures.

Create a synthetic transaction and commit it.

Restart or allow the compute endpoint to suspend where the service permits.

Reconnect and verify that the committed record remains available.

Create a second transaction and roll it back. Verify that the rolled-back record is absent.

Create a branch and verify that the parent and child diverge after a child write.

Generate a Lakebase update and measure when it becomes available in Delta.

Run reconciliation at a matched watermark.

Record observed recovery and integration times. Do not convert a single test into a universal SLA.

Use Lakebase for customer-facing or operational applications that need PostgreSQL compatibility, constraints, transactions, point reads, writes, and branches.

Use Delta or Iceberg for large historical datasets, market data, risk factors, feature engineering, surveillance histories, and large aggregations.

Use Photon through Databricks SQL for compatible analytical workloads.

Use Lakehouse//RT where available for low-latency, high-concurrency analytical serving over governed lakehouse tables.

Use Lakebase Change Data Feed to expose selected operational changes to Delta without operating a separate external CDC stack.

Define one authoritative owner for each field. Avoid independent writes to the same business field in both PostgreSQL and Delta.

Define consistency requirements by use case:

Create separate development, test, performance, disaster-recovery, and production environments.

Configure identity federation, private connectivity, network controls, secret management, audit delivery, service principals, and least-privilege PostgreSQL roles.

Configure high availability at the compute layer according to the required recovery-time objective.

Configure regional disaster recovery according to the jurisdiction and business-continuity plan.

Define data-retention requirements for branches, WAL-derived history, Delta history, analytical snapshots, and regulated records.

Load-test PostgreSQL transactions, page-cache miss behavior, connection pooling, branch creation, integration freshness, Photon analysis, reconciliation, and application concurrency.

Test compute failure, integration delay, schema change, duplicate delivery, out-of-order updates, branch misuse, stale analytical data, and unavailable market data.

Retain independent order, execution, broker, clearing, settlement, and ledger records where required. A unified architecture does not remove independent reconciliation obligations.

Lakebase separates PostgreSQL compute from durable storage. Compute remains familiar to PostgreSQL applications, while Safekeepers, Pageservers, and cloud object storage maintain durable and versioned state.

Safekeepers are responsible for durable WAL replication. Pageservers organize page history and reconstruct pages at requested LSNs.

Image layers reduce reconstruction work by providing page snapshots. Delta layers preserve changes between snapshots. Compaction controls layer depth and storage efficiency.

Branches share historical storage and diverge through copy-on-write. They are useful for development, incident reproduction, and model testing, but they are not full Git repositories.

LTAP removes much of the fragile external integration stack between an operational PostgreSQL system and analytics. It does not justify claims of literal zero processing, zero latency, or automatic synchronous Parquet conversion on every PostgreSQL commit.

Institutional systems should record source commit positions, integration watermarks, market timestamps, and analytical cutoffs. That is how front-office and back-office users understand whether two results represent the same point in time.

A consensus-label failure occurs when an undocumented Paxos or Raft implementation is presented as a product guarantee. Use the documented concept of quorum-based replication unless Databricks specifies the protocol.

A local-NVMe assumption occurs when a design depends on Safekeeper local hardware details that are not part of the customer contract.

A direct-Parquet assumption occurs when applications expect every PostgreSQL commit to synchronously produce Delta or Iceberg files. Use the supported LTAP integration and measure its freshness.

A private-format dependency occurs when applications depend on internal layer files, key encodings, or Pageserver indexes. Use supported PostgreSQL, Lakebase, Unity Catalog, and Delta interfaces.

An unlimited-time-travel assumption occurs when historical data is expected forever. Configure and test retention and archival.

An absolute-synchronization assumption occurs when operational data, market data, and risk results are described as perfectly simultaneous. Record and compare watermarks and timestamps.

A branch-is-backup assumption occurs when branches replace backup, archival, and disaster recovery. They serve different purposes.

A Free Edition assumption occurs when a learning environment is treated as a production transactional platform. Move to a supported paid environment before processing real institutional data.

Beyond Building Apps: How to Build a TikTok Content Engine That Drives Real Users

📅 Nov 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Building a mobile app is only half the job.

You can spend months developing features, polishing the UI, fixing bugs, and releasing updates. But if nobody discovers your app, all that development effort has limited business value.

One of the biggest challenges for indie developers and small software teams is distribution.

How do you consistently get your product in front of the right people without spending thousands of dollars on advertising?

One approach worth exploring is building a repeatable short-form content engine using TikTok, Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts, and Facebook Reels.

The goal isn't simply to get millions of views. It's to turn attention into app installations, active users, and eventually paying customers.

Here is how I would approach building that system.

One common mistake is opening TikTok and immediately starting to create random videos.

A better approach is to study what is already working.

Search for topics related to your app category and analyze successful creators.

For example, if you're marketing a productivity app, research:

Don't just watch videos for entertainment. Study their structure.

The objective is to identify repeatable patterns, not copy somebody else's content.

Instead of reinventing the wheel for every video, develop a library of content formats.

Start with a relatable problem and demonstrate a practical solution.

Present an interesting situation, build curiosity, and deliver an unexpected conclusion.

Show the difference between doing something manually and using a better workflow.

Break down useful information into short, visually engaging slides.

Present a situation that your target audience immediately recognizes.

Share surprising but accurate information related to your app category.

Show how your application solves a real problem rather than simply listing its features.

Each format serves a different purpose. Some attract viewers, while others generate product interest.

A viewer decides very quickly whether a video is worth watching.

That makes the opening hook one of the most important parts of the entire production process.

"Today I want to show you our new productivity application."

"You're probably wasting 30 minutes every day doing this manually."

A good hook creates curiosity, identifies a problem, or promises a useful outcome.

However, the rest of the video must deliver on that promise. Misleading hooks might generate clicks but damage trust and retention.

Not every video needs a camera, presenter, or expensive production setup.

Slideshow content can be an effective format for educational and storytelling content.

"5 things I wish I knew before starting my own business."

Introduce the situation and why it matters.

"Save this for later" or "Explore the tool in our profile."

A good slideshow needs more than attractive images. It needs a logical progression, readable typography, strong visual hierarchy, and a reason to continue to the next slide.

For production, AI tools can help with research, scriptwriting, image generation, narration, and visual preparation.

The important part is maintaining editorial quality rather than publishing automatically generated slides without reviewing them.

This is where the process becomes scalable.

Instead of creating one video from beginning to end every day, separate production into stages.

The best automation strategy is to automate repetitive production tasks while keeping human review for accuracy, originality, and quality.

One important lesson in managing multiple accounts is that publishing identical videos everywhere is not a sustainable content strategy.

You can reuse a research topic, but create genuinely different executions.

For example, one topic can produce five distinct videos:

Each version should have its own hook, script, visual presentation, and narrative approach.

This makes content production more efficient without turning the accounts into duplicate-content distribution channels.

Also, adapt content to the requirements and audience expectations of each platform.

This is especially important for mobile app developers.

People generally open TikTok to discover entertaining, educational, or interesting content. They are not necessarily looking for another app advertisement.

A better approach is to lead with the audience's problem.

For example, imagine you're marketing a photo-editing application.

"Ever taken a great photo only to notice something distracting in the background?"

The application becomes part of the story rather than the entire story.

Different videos can have different objectives:

Use direct CTAs when the content genuinely demonstrates a relevant benefit. In other videos, a softer CTA or no promotional CTA may be more appropriate.

Views alone don't tell you whether your marketing is working.

A video with 100,000 views and no meaningful product interest might be less valuable than one with 5,000 views that generates actual installations.

If your business primarily targets the US market, monitor the percentage of viewers coming from the United States.

TikTok Studio provides audience and content analytics, although available metrics can vary by account and feature.

Remember that a US-focused proxy or device configuration does not guarantee US distribution. Audience relevance, viewer behavior, content language, and other recommendation signals matter.

Don't immediately assume that your account is shadowbanned.

If views are good but engagement is weak:

If engagement is good but there are no app installations:

Treat each underperforming video as information that can improve the next experiment.

Avoid fake engagement, mutual likes, artificial views, and follow exchanges. These practices can put multiple accounts at risk and do not create real customers.

A sustainable content engine needs regular experimentation.

Study successful videos, competitors, topics, and emerging formats.

Create scripts, hooks, and a weekly content calendar.

Generate visuals, slideshows, voiceovers, and edited videos.

Publish original content and monitor early performance.

Compare retention, engagement, profile visits, and app acquisition.

Identify winning formats, improve weak videos, and prepare the next batch.

The exact schedule can change depending on team capacity. Consistency and learning are more important than following a rigid calendar.

There are two very different ways to approach content marketing.

"How can we reach people who genuinely need our product?"

The second question leads to better business decisions.

For mobile app developers, the complete process should look like this:

Research → Create → Publish → Analyze → Optimize → Acquire Users → Generate Revenue.

Content marketing is not a one-time campaign. It is an ongoing system.

You will publish videos that fail. Some formats will work better than others. Certain topics will attract attention but produce no conversions.

The objective is to learn from every experiment and gradually build a repeatable process.

Building an application is an engineering challenge.

Getting people to discover, understand, trust, and pay for that application is a distribution challenge.

Developers should spend more time understanding their audiences, studying successful content, testing different creative formats, and building systems that make consistent publishing possible.

You need a reliable process that repeatedly puts your product in front of the right people.

Build the product. Build the audience. Build the distribution system.

That is how development turns into a sustainable business.

What has worked best for your app marketing: educational videos, storytelling, slideshows, or direct product demonstrations? I'd love to hear what other indie developers are experimenting with.

Binance Secures In-Principle Approval in Gelephu Mindfulness City, Plans Asia Hub in Bhutan

📅 Nov 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

The regulatory milestone marks a major step toward Binance establishing an Asia hub in Gelephu Mindfulness City, alongside commitments to create jobs and strengthen Bhutan's digital-asset capabilities

BANGKOK, Nov. 28, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Binance, the leading global financial platform powered by blockchain, has received in-principle approval (IPA) from the Gelephu Central Bank (GCB) to establish regulated digital-asset operations in Gelephu Mindfulness City (GMC), Bhutan.

The milestone was marked at Binance Blockchain Week 2026, where Binance and GMC signed a cooperation agreement setting out their broader partnership and plans for GMC to become an Asia hub for Binance users. The IPA is an important milestone in a broader, ongoing effort to expand access and build out the ecosystem locally. Binance has been deepening its presence in Bhutan since launching a national crypto-powered tourism payment system in 2025. As the partnership progresses, Binance will continue building out the local digital-asset ecosystem.

Binance will now work with GCB to fulfil the conditions attached to the IPA and complete the remaining regulatory requirements before receiving its full licence.

The partnership goes beyond licensing. Binance plans to establish a substantive operational presence in Bhutan, creating employment opportunities while investing in the development of talent and digital-asset capabilities.

As part of the partnership, Binance will work with GMC to build capabilities and upskill the talent pool, including through employment, training, knowledge sharing and collaboration across areas such as digital assets, compliance and operations. The parties also intend to explore opportunities to develop GMC as a regional centre of excellence, supporting Binance's broader operations in Asia while building expertise and capabilities within GMC.

Speaking on this milestone, Jigdrel Singay, Board Director of Gelephu Mindfulness City, said "Binance choosing Gelephu Mindfulness City as a base for its Asia operations is an important milestone for what we are building in Bhutan. Our ambition is not simply to attract global companies to establish an entity here. We want them to build real operations, create meaningful jobs, develop talent and transfer capabilities that remain in the country over the long term.

"The in-principle approval is an important first step, and we look forward to working closely with Binance and GCB as Binance completes the remaining regulatory requirements and builds its presence in GMC," Singay added.

SB Seker Head of APAC, Binance said, "Establishing an Asia hub in Gelephu Mindfulness City is a strategic decision that reflects Binance's commitment to operating within clear, progressive regulatory frameworks. The IPA from GCB is an important validation of GMC's approach to digital asset regulation, one that protects users while enabling innovation."

"GMC's vision of combining traditional values with cutting-edge technology, powered by renewable energy, makes it an ideal location for Binance's regional center of excellence. We are committed to making this partnership a model for responsible growth in the digital asset sector," added Seker.

The partnership forms part of GMC's broader ambition to establish Bhutan as a trusted and internationally connected hub for digital assets and financial innovation, combining a clear regulatory framework with a long-term focus on developing local talent and institutional capabilities.

The granting of the IPA does not constitute a full licence. Binance must satisfy the conditions specified by GCB and complete the remaining regulatory requirements before the relevant regulated activities may commence.

About Gelephu Mindfulness City: The Gelephu Mindfulness City Special Administrative Region is a visionary initiative creating a world-class economic hub in southern Bhutan, centered on mindfulness, sustainability, and innovation. The SAR integrates traditional Bhutanese values with globally recognized legal frameworks, cutting-edge design and technology, while harnessing the Kingdom's abundant renewable energy resources to serve as a global exemplar of holistic development. For more information, visit www.gmc.bt.

About Binance: Binance is a leading global financial platform, combining advanced technology and AI to connect users and institutions with the next generation of finance. Trusted by more than 300 million users across 100+ countries, Binance brings together a broad range of financial products and services, connecting digital assets with traditional financial markets through one integrated platform. Beyond financial services, its ecosystem extends to education, research, social impact, institutional solutions and Web3 innovation. Powered by industry-leading technology, advanced AI capabilities, deep liquidity, robust security and a commitment to compliance, Binance is building an inclusive global financial ecosystem to realise its vision of increasing the freedom of money for people around the world. For more information, visit: https://www.binance.com

Il Venezia c’è, l’attacco meno: la lezione di Juan Jesus, Nicola in trincea e le idee per gennaio

📅 Nov 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Davide Nicola va in trincea per i propri attaccanti. Ha spiegato che non esiste alcun "problema del gol" e che non si può pretendere di avere attaccanti che garantiscano numeri tanto migliori fin da subito, perché altrimenti questi ultimi non si troverebbero in squadre che lottano per salvarsi. "I numeri noi dobbiamo costruirceli", ripete Nicola fin dal suo arrivo. Come sempre, l'allenatore del Venezia pensa solo ed esclusivamente al lavoro di campo, a migliorare chi ha a disposizione, a tenere alto il morale dei suoi.

Intorno a lui c'è chi dovrà fare le dovute riflessioni (sui giocatori) da qui a gennaio, in base alle risposte che arriveranno dal lavoro di cui parla Nicola. Il prossimo mese dovrà essere un banco di prova per dimostrare di valere la Serie A. Nessuno è stato messo in discussone o in preallarme per eventuali cessioni: ora si pensa al campo. Ma le prime idee in entrata iniziano ad arrivare: da Bonazzoli fino a Dovbyk. Tutto dipenderà da quali di questi nomi potranno trasformarsi in reali occasioni a gennaio: nel calcio cambia tutto da una settimana all'altra ecco perché sarà pure difficile portarsi avanti.

Nelle scorse settimane si è parlato pressoché solo di Adams, come problema. Ma è lecito chiedersi per esempio se Yeboah saprà scuotersi per iniziare a incidere anche in A, visto che con il Bologna ha sbagliato una chance enorme. Rrahmani saprà convincere Nicola di meritare più spazio? Lauberbach sta giocando, ma è ancora a secco e pure lui ieri ha fallito una chance. Adorante freme, anche lui avrà modo di far vedere di potersi far valere anche in massima serie dopo aver fatto bene in B. Insomma, per una volta è giusto non gettare la croce su Adams, che peraltro ieri ha mandato in porta due compagni.

Una lezione importante è arrivata da capitan Juan Jesus. Con tanta lucidità, calma e schiettezza, senza tanti giri di parole. "Le occasioni le stiamo creando. Dobbiamo essere più bravi a gestire i palloni negli ultimi metri, gli attaccanti hanno 5-6 occasioni a partita e dobbiamo iniziare ad approfittare delle occasioni che abbiamo", ha detto in conferenza stampa.

Ancora più interessante la sua riflessione sulle critiche ricevute dai compagni in attacco e sul momento di difficoltà che stanno attraversando: "Innanzitutto si sbaglia perché si prova. Quando si sprecano occasioni ci sta che ci sia un dispiacere, una delusione, ma il nostro lavoro è anche questo: subire le critiche e continuare a lavorare".

Chi si allena con Juan Jesus potrà solo che imparare da queste parole: lui di critiche ne ha dovute sopportare, ma ai massimi livelli e in squadre di livello mondiale. Il messaggio sembra essere: non nascondiamoci, ma prendiamo di petto critiche e problemi perché è ora di reagire, non di autocommiserarsi.

E ha spiegato anche il come: "Lavorando. Per esempio mettendosi meglio con il corpo quando si riceve la palla, facendo uno stop in più... Sono ragazzi giovani, stanno facendo del loro meglio. Il gruppo è sano. Dispiace comunque, non vediamo l'ora che trovino continuità nel segnare". E dopo l'analisi, ha chiosato: "Penso che con quello che stiamo facendo ci sarà un bel traguardo alla fine della stagione, sono sereno su questo, possiamo fare la storia". Il Venezia c'è e può ancora salvarsi, ora deve trovare i gol per farlo.

Feeling the tension? Try this doctor-approved mobility workout to release aches and stiffness

If you regularly wake up feeling stiff, notice your hips tightening after sitting for too long, or find that everyday movements leave you feeling achy, it might be time to pay attention to your mobility. While some changes in flexibility and joint movement are a natural part of aging, aches, stiffness and tension don't have to become something you put up with.

One of the best ways to keep your body moving comfortably is to make mobility work a priority. Gentle, controlled movements take your joints through their range of motion, help maintain flexibility and strengthen the muscles that support everyday movement. You don't need to spend hours stretching to see the benefits — a short routine practised regularly can be a better way to build the habit.

With that in mind, I asked Dr. Gaby Van Sickle, physical therapist and co-founder of Functional Physical Therapy, to share a 10-minute mobility workout she recommends to her clients. The routine combines simple movements to keep your hips, knees and ankles moving, build lower-body strength and support the balance and coordination we rely on as we age.

So, if you're looking for a practical way to ease stiffness and keep those everyday aches and pains at bay, here's how to fit 10 minutes of mobility into your day.

Why: Van Sickle recommends starting with walking because it’s the ideal way to prepare the body for movement. “It gradually increases blood flow to the muscles, and encourages movement through the hips, knees, ankles, and spine,” she says. “It’ll also help reduce the sensation of stiffness before beginning more targeted mobility exercises.”

Time: 1 minute Reps: 4-6 per move in each direction

Why: “Maintaining mobility in all directions of the cervical spine is important for everyday activities like driving, looking up at objects and reading,” Van Sickle explains. “Gentle neck movements like this can also help reduce stiffness associated with prolonged sitting.”

Time: 1 minute Reps: 10 in each direction

Why: Shoulder rolls are the ideal addition to your longevity toolkit. “They help improve mobility through the shoulders and upper back, which makes movements like reaching overhead and getting dressed easier,” Van Sickle says. Over time, they’ll help ease aching in the shoulders and neck.

Why: Neck and lower back stiffness are common, and it’s usually caused by too much pressure or tension in this area. “Thoracic rotations help relieve this by distributing movement throughout the trunk,” Van Sickle explains.

Why: These are great to do after prolonged periods of sitting, as they “promote movement through the spine and pelvis, helping to reduce any stiffness.”

Time: 1 minute Reps: 8-10 of each movement per leg

Why: Van Sickle recommends these moves frequently to her clients because they promote active hip mobility while strengthening the gluteal muscles. Keeping the hips mobile and the surrounding muscles strong can help reduce feelings of stiffness and make everyday movements, like walking and stepping to the side, feel more comfortable.

Why: “This is a functional movement that promotes mobility and strength through the core, hips, knees, and ankles,” Van Sickle says. Staying active in these areas helps reduce stiffness in the lower body.

Why: Stiff ankles and tight lower-leg muscles can make walking feel less comfortable. Practicing calf raises and toe raises moves the ankle in both directions while strengthening the muscles around it, which will help support a smoother, more comfortable stride.

Time: 1 minute Reps: 15-30 marches per leg

Why: Standing marches gently move the hips and knees while encouraging you to shift your weight from one leg to the other. “It’s about keeping the lower body moving to ease feelings of stiffness after periods of sitting or inactivity,” Van Sickle advocates.

If aches, stiffness and tension are making everyday movement feel more difficult, a regular mobility routine can help. These exercises gently move your hips, knees and ankles through their range of motion while strengthening the muscles that support your joints, helping you maintain the mobility, balance and strength you need as you age.

The key is consistency, rather than pushing yourself to do more. Try setting aside 10 minutes each day to work through the routine, moving slowly and staying within a comfortable range of motion. Over time, a regular practice can help you feel less stiff after periods of inactivity and more confident with everyday movements.

The 4 secret Amazon clearance sites you should check before buying retail

📅 Nov 28, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

As we power toward the holidays, the shopping pressure is officially on. Your natural instinct may be to type what you need into the Amazon search bar, click the first Prime-eligible result, and pay whatever price the algorithm spits out. That’s a huge mistake.

Amazon buries its best discounts on purpose. The retail giant operates three distinct clearance portals where you can score open-box electronics, overstocked gifts, and refurbished tech for up to 70% off retail. Before you pay full price for holiday gifts this year, here’s where you actually need to look.

Amazon Resale

Formerly known as Amazon Warehouse, Amazon Resale is where Amazon sends customer returns. The trick to using Resale is understanding its strict grading system.

If you buy an item rated as Used—Like New, it means the product itself is in perfect, untouched condition, but the original shrink wrap is broken or the cardboard box has a minor dent.

You get a massive discount simply because the packaging isn’t pretty enough to sit on a retail shelf. If you’re buying tech gear or kitchen appliances where the box just goes straight into the recycling bin anyway, it’s the easiest way to save hundreds. Just stick strictly to the Like New or Very Good tiers.

Amazon Outlet

Unlike Resale, everything in Amazon Outlet is brand new. This is where Amazon dumps seasonal overstock and excess inventory that’s taking up too much physical space in its fulfillment centers.

Finding it is the hard part. It isn’t advertised on the home page. You have to type amazon.com/outlet directly into your browser or dig deep through the Deals and Savings menu on the mobile app.

Once you’re in, you’ll find everything from holiday decorations to winter apparel marked down by 50% to 70%. It’s the absolute best spot to hunt for stocking stuffers and white elephant gifts without breaking the bank.

Woot

Amazon bought Woot back in 2010, but it still operates as a standalone site at woot.com. It’s a dedicated daily deal platform that runs flash sales on electronics, tools, and apparel until the inventory sells out.

If you’re hunting for a refurbished television, a discounted sound bar, or cheap smart home gear, Woot should be your first stop every morning. The checkout system is fully integrated, meaning your Prime membership still gets you free shipping. Just be prepared to act fast, because the best tech deals usually vanish before your morning coffee gets cold.

Amazon Haul

If you’ve ever been tempted to buy cheap stocking stuffers off Temu or Shein but didn’t want to hand your credit card to an overseas app, you’ll be interested to know that Amazon built a direct competitor right inside its own ecosystem.

It’s called Amazon Haul, and the gimmick is simple: Every item comes from outside the U.S., which often means cheaper, direct-from-manufacturer pricing.

Free shipping kicks in once you hit $25; less than that, and there’s a $4 shipping charge per order. While you lose next-day delivery—items can take up to a couple of weeks to arrive—and the return window drops to just 15 days, every purchase is still backed by Amazon. That makes it a safer way to buy ultra-cheap phone cases, kitchen gadgets, and holiday party supplies without risking a scam.

Alle ore 17:15, lo stadio "Romeo Menti" ospita la sfida tra L.R. Vicenza e Cesena, gara valevole per la 14ª giornata del campionato di Serie BKT. L'incontro mette di fronte due formazioni che vivono momenti diametralmente opposti in classifica: i biancorossi, penultimi con 10 punti, affrontano i romagnoli, sesti a quota 21 in piena zona playoff. I numeri raccontano di una sfida dalle tendenze statistiche ben definite.

Il Vicenza presenta finora la difesa più battuta del torneo con 27 reti subite in 13 giornate (16 quelle realizzate) e fatica in particolare tra le mura amiche, dove ha raccolto appena 1 vittoria, 1 pareggio e 4 sconfitte, perdendo le ultime tre gare interne consecutive.

Il Cesena viaggia invece a una media di 1,62 punti a partita (19 gol fatti e 15 incassati) ed è imbattuto da cinque turni, nei quali ha ottenuto quattro vittorie e un pareggio.

La tradizione storica recente sorride tuttavia ai veneti: negli ultimi cinque scontri diretti ufficiali tra Serie B e Serie C il Vicenza è rimasto imbattuto con due vittorie e tre pareggi (tra cui i due 0-0 nei playoff di Serie C del maggio 2023), mentre il "Menti" si è storicamente rivelato un campo ostico per i bianconeri.

La sconfitta interna per 0-1 contro la Carrarese nel turno infrasettimanale ha segnato l'epilogo della gestione di Fabio Gallo, esonerato dalla società dopo aver raccolto due sole vittorie in tredici giornate. Per risalire la china il club ha affidato la panchina a Davide Dionigi, chiamato al debutto immediato in una gara ad alto coefficiente di difficoltà. Il nuovo tecnico dovrà lavorare soprattutto sulla tenuta difensiva e sulla gestione dei secondi tempi, visto che i veneti hanno incassato 12 gol da fine ottobre in poi.

COME ARRIVA IL CESENA - Clima diametralmente opposto in casa romagnola, dove l'entusiasmo è alle stelle dopo la larga vittoria per 5-1 inflitta all'Ascoli nel turno infrasettimanale. La squadra, allenata da Alessandro Diamanti, arriva in Veneto, forte di una striscia di tre successi consecutivi (contro Catanzaro, Hellas Verona e Ascoli) che l'ha proiettata al sesto posto in graduatoria, a una sola lunghezza dal terzo posto occupato da Avellino e Mantova. Il trascinatore assoluto dei bianconeri è Cristian Shpendi: reduce da una tripletta contro i marchigiani, l'attaccante ha già raggiunto quota 12 reti in 13 partite, confermandosi il capocannoniere del campionato.

Con la squadra in salute, nessun giocatore squalificato e un rendimento esterno solido (2 vittorie, 2 pareggi e 2 sconfitte finora lontano dal "Manuzzi"), i romagnoli puntano a sfatare il tabù del "Menti" per consolidare la propria candidatura nelle zone nobili della classifica.
