Scientists identify two ages when children may be most vulnerable to screen time

📅 Nov 27, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Screen time at certain ages may be more closely tied to children's future learning and memory than previously recognized. A new study tracking children from age 1 to 8 found that those who spent more time watching screens during infancy and around the start of elementary school tended to perform worse academically at age 9 and have weaker working memory at age 10.5.

The findings suggest that when children use screens may be just as important as how much time they spend in front of them. Two ages in particular, 1 and 6, emerged as potentially sensitive periods in childhood development.

As digital devices become an increasingly common part of childhood, understanding their potential long-term effects has become a growing priority. Recommendations from the World Health Organization (WHO) and the American Academy of Pediatrics generally emphasize avoiding screen exposure during the first 18 to 24 months of life and limiting it to less than one hour a day for children ages 2 to 5. However, many young children spend considerably more time using screens.

Tracking Screen Time Throughout Childhood

Despite growing concerns about children's digital habits, previous research has produced mixed findings about the relationship between screen time and cognitive development. Many earlier studies examined children at a single point in time, concentrated on children already attending school, or did not regularly track screen habits throughout early childhood.

Following the same children over several years allows researchers to investigate whether screen exposure at particular ages is more strongly associated with later outcomes. This approach can also help researchers better account for the influence of family circumstances and environmental factors.

Scientists from Inserm and the National University of Singapore addressed these gaps in a study published in the World Journal of Pediatrics. The researchers examined data from 502 children participating in the Growing Up in Singapore Towards healthy Outcomes (GUSTO) birth cohort.

Parents reported their children's screen viewing habits at six different points between infancy and middle childhood. The researchers then evaluated the children's academic achievement and working memory several years later.

Working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and manipulate information. It plays an essential role in everyday learning, allowing children to follow instructions, solve math problems, understand sentences, and keep track of information while completing tasks.

The researchers found that greater screen exposure at certain stages of childhood was associated with lower academic achievement and poorer working memory later in life. These relationships were particularly consistent among children who spent more time watching screens at age 1 and around age 6, when formal schooling typically begins.

Children who accumulated more screen time throughout childhood also tended to achieve lower academic scores. However, the strength of the associations varied depending on when the exposure occurred, suggesting that some developmental stages may be more sensitive than others.

One possible explanation is that screen viewing can take time away from activities that support cognitive development, including conversations with caregivers, imaginative play, and hands-on exploration of the physical world. These experiences provide opportunities for children to develop language, attention, memory, and problem-solving skills.

"The effect sizes we saw at age 1 were the largest among all time points we examined," the authors said. "That suggests early infancy may be a window of heightened sensitivity, when the developing brain is particularly vulnerable to the displacement of learning interactions by screen time. We were also surprised to see that while screen use at age 2 and 3 did not show significant links, the associations re-emerged at age 6 -- when children enter formal schooling. So it is not just about early years; screen use later in childhood still matters."

Although the study identifies associations rather than proving that screen time directly causes poorer cognitive or academic outcomes, the results highlight the potential importance of managing children's screen habits at different ages.

Why Even Small Differences in Screen Time Matter

According to the researchers, the results reinforce the principle that "less is better" when it comes to children's screen time.

An additional hour of daily screen viewing may not produce a noticeable difference in an individual child's academic abilities. However, when similar patterns occur across a large population, even relatively small differences in average performance could increase the number of children who experience academic difficulties.

The researchers suggest that efforts to encourage healthier screen habits could begin during infancy, with renewed emphasis around the transition to elementary school. This approach recognizes that children's developmental needs continue to change well beyond their toddler years.

The authors also stress that the amount of time children spend in front of screens is only one part of a much larger picture. Future studies should investigate whether the quality of digital content, the types of devices children use, and whether parents watch and interact with their children during screen time influence developmental outcomes.

Understanding these differences could eventually help researchers develop more targeted recommendations that consider not only how much screen time children get, but also when and how they engage with digital technology.

The GUSTO study was supported by the Singapore National Research Foundation and the Singapore Ministry of Health's National Medical Research Council (NMRC/TCR/004-NUS/2008 and NMRC/TCR/012-NUHS/2014). Additional funding came from the Agence Nationale de la Recherche (ANR) in France (iSCAN project, ANR-20-CE36-0001).

Mentre navighi nell'app, scorri il dito da sinistra a destra dello schermo per tornare alle pagine precedenti

Luciano Spalletti, allenatore della Juventus, ha parlato ai microfoni di Sky Sport dopo il successo per 4-1 dei bianconeri in Europa League contro l'Omonia Nicosia.

Di seguito le dichiarazioni del tecnico della Juve dalla pancia dell'Allianz Stadium.

"All'inizio abbiamo commesso un paio di incertezze che gli avversari hanno sfruttato. Naturalmente questo complica la possibilità di esprimere al meglio le proprie qualità, perché senti la pressione e il timore di subire un contropiede o qualcosa del genere. Poi Cambiaso ha rimesso un po' a posto le cose con quel grande gol e da lì la squadra ha giocato con maggiore tranquillità".

AI made self-hosting fun again

📅 Nov 26, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Jan-Lukas ElseTech, life and everything else

I’ve been self-hosting things for many years. There were times when I was quite enthusiastic about it, constantly trying out new software and tinkering with my infrastructure. But at some point, that enthusiasm faded a bit.I never really stopped self-hosting, but I became less inclined to experiment with new things. Maintaining what I already had running was enough for me.Over the last few months, however, I’ve found myself getting increasingly excited about self-hosting again. And, somewhat ironically, AI is a big reason for that.Less frictionMost of my infrastructure configuration lives in Git repositories, mainly in the form of Docker Compose files, scripts, and other configuration files. This makes it possible to use AI coding agents to work on my infrastructure in much the same way as they would work on any other software project.Whenever I want to try a new service, adjust an existing configuration, or automate something, I can now do so with considerably less effort.In the past, I would sometimes put off certain changes simply because I didn’t feel like spending an evening reading changelogs and documentation or troubleshooting issues. It’s not that I couldn’t have done these things before. But often, the amount of effort required just wasn’t worth it to me.Now, even relatively spontaneous ideas often end up becoming reality.Trying things I always found interestingThere are also technologies that I’ve always found interesting but never felt knowledgeable enough about to really make use of them.NixOS is a good example. I’ve always liked the idea of declaratively configuring an entire system; I even used it on my laptop during my Linux honeymoon phase. But getting everything configured the way I wanted was quite a hurdle. With the help of AI, I’m now making much more extensive use of NixOS on my home server.For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time).Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. Without AI, it would probably have taken me at least a week.AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations.Automating almost everythingSomething I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, update, and deployment processes for my infrastructure.A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of new releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly.I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary.With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa.Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything.Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing.And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or update a service.Back to more powerful hardwareAs I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server.For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though.I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. Noise was the main reason I switched to the t640 in the first place.It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely new machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site.Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life.Building my own toolsBut it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by big tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

It’s not that I couldn’t have done these things before. But often, the amount of effort required just wasn’t worth it to me.Now, even relatively spontaneous ideas often end up becoming reality.Trying things I always found interestingThere are also technologies that I’ve always found interesting but never felt knowledgeable enough about to really make use of them.NixOS is a good example. I’ve always liked the idea of declaratively configuring an entire system; I even used it on my laptop during my Linux honeymoon phase. But getting everything configured the way I wanted was quite a hurdle. With the help of AI, I’m now making much more extensive use of NixOS on my home server.For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time).Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. Without AI, it would probably have taken me at least a week.AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations.Automating almost everythingSomething I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, update, and deployment processes for my infrastructure.A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of new releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly.I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary.With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa.Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything.Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing.And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or update a service.Back to more powerful hardwareAs I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server.For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though.I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. Noise was the main reason I switched to the t640 in the first place.It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely new machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site.Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life.Building my own toolsBut it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by big tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by big tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time).Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. Without AI, it would probably have taken me at least a week.AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations.Automating almost everythingSomething I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, update, and deployment processes for my infrastructure.A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of new releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly.I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary.With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa.Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything.Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing.And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or update a service.Back to more powerful hardwareAs I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server.For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though.I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. Noise was the main reason I switched to the t640 in the first place.It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely new machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site.Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life.Building my own toolsBut it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by big tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa.Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything.Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing.And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or update a service.Back to more powerful hardwareAs I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server.For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though.I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. Noise was the main reason I switched to the t640 in the first place.It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely new machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site.Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely new machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site.Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life.Building my own toolsBut it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by big tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

Scientists find a new way to study some of the ocean’s most elusive microbes

📅 Nov 26, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

A new study sheds light on the largely unexplored microbial world beneath the ocean and its potential ecological significance.

Most of the microbes living on the deep seafloor have never grown in a lab dish. On the way to the surface, a sample loses the high pressure and steady cold its microbes are adapted to.

The sudden change can kill the microbes before anyone gets to study them.

A robotic system called DISCUSS keeps both conditions in place, from the seafloor all the way to the lab bench where single microbes are picked out. With it, a team grew a bacterium that barely grows at ordinary air pressure.

The work was led by Jing-Chun Feng of Guangdong University of Technology in China. Zhengguang Liu, a researcher in the University of Manchester Department of Chemical Engineering, was one of the paper’s corresponding authors.

“Scientists have long struggled to grow many microorganisms found in nature under laboratory conditions, limiting our understanding of how they live and function,” said Liu.

The deep sea is home to a vast diversity of microbes, many of which have adapted to extreme pressure and near-freezing temperatures.

Some deep-sea microbes even produce enzymes and other molecules.

The molecules that deep-sea microbes create can be useful for medicines, new materials, food and energy.

Scientists say that less than one percent of deep-sea microbes can be grown with normal lab techniques.

“Deep-sea microbes are particularly fascinating because they have evolved to survive extreme pressure, cold and unusual chemical conditions,” Liu said.

The testing of this technology was carried out in the South China Sea at a depth of 4,300 feet (1,300 meters) in a cold seep location.

Cold seeps are areas of the seafloor where methane and other compounds emerge at temperatures similar to those of the surrounding water.

At this depth, the water pressure would be 1,900 pounds per square inch (13 megapascals), which is about 130 times the atmospheric pressure at sea level, and water temperature would be 39°F (4°C).

Before carrying out any sampling procedure, sensors detected the levels of methane, carbon dioxide, oxygen, acidity, temperature, and pressure on the seafloor.

After evaluation by the software, only those locations with scores related to methanotrophic microbes were sampled.

The sealed samplers kept more than 98% of the seafloor pressure on the way up.

In the lab, the system built a virtual copy of the seafloor conditions from the sensor readings. Researchers call that kind of copy a digital twin, and the machine used it as the target to hold.

When a sample moved from one chamber to the next, one pump pushed while another pulled at a matched rate. That kept the pressure from jumping during the handoff.

To grow one kind of microbe on its own, a microbiologist spreads cells thinly across a soft gel. Each cell that survives grows into a small dot called a colony.

DISCUSS performs this task inside a sealed, high‑pressure chamber. A robot arm spreads the cells with a needle, and a camera watches through a sapphire window.

A force sensor in the arm lets it press lightly enough not to tear the gel. In tests, the camera software recognized colonies with 94.6% accuracy.

The needle hit its target within 0.002 inches of the intended spot. Between tasks, the system sterilized the needle using light, keeping the pressure seal intact.

“From an engineering perspective, what excites me most is how intelligent sensing, modeling and automation can help us explore biological systems that were previously difficult to study,” said Liu.

The team recovered 34 microbes and grew each one on its own.

In 11 of them, a gene that scientists use to tell microbes apart differed enough from known reference strains that they may belong to groups not yet described.

The team took a close look at two of the 34. Both turned out to be strains of known species.

One belongs to Pseudomonas songnenensis, and the other, named HP_SR10, belongs to Bacillus cereus.

To test how much each strain depended on pressure, the researchers grew both for 11 days at five pressures, from ordinary air pressure to a little above the seafloor’s.

The Pseudomonas strain grew about as well at ordinary air pressure as it did at seafloor pressure. HP_SR10 didn’t. It grew best at the same pressure as the seep it came from, and poorly at ordinary air pressure.

The authors wrote that this strain can’t be recovered with conventional methods, which grow microbes at surface pressure.

The system also kept a whole community of microbes alive and working for 180 days.

At its center was a partnership between methane-eating archaea, single-celled microbes distinct from bacteria, and bacteria that use sulfate from seawater.

Pumps fed the community methane and nutrients and flushed out waste. That kept sulfide, a byproduct that holds these microbes back at high levels, below 4 millimoles per liter.

Around day 110, both partners became noticeably more common.

The authors wrote that communities like this one typically collapse in closed lab containers with no fresh supply.

Carbon made near the ocean surface can sink to the deep ocean, and scientists still don’t fully understand how deep-sea microbes change it.

Growing a wider range of these microbes under conditions close to home could help scientists study that process.

Only two of the 34 microbes were studied in detail. The study doesn’t describe what the 11 possibly new microbes do, or whether any make useful molecules.

All of the samples also came from a single seep. The authors noted that the design could be adapted for deeper water and for very hot places such as hydrothermal vents.

Next, the team plans to run many plates at once under different conditions and to track dissolved chemicals more closely as they change.

The researchers also plan to automate growing microbes in liquid instead of on gel.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Sensors.

Principles Don't Ship: Making Responsible AI an Operating Practice

📅 Nov 26, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Posted on Nov 26 • Originally published at linkedin.com

Almost every large organisation now has a set of responsible AI principles. They are usually well written. Fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy, safety, human oversight. They sit on a web page, they were approved by a committee, and they are referenced in board papers.

Then a team ships an AI feature, and nobody can point to the moment where any of those principles changed a decision. There was no test that could have failed. There was no review with the authority to stop the release. There was no metric that would have revealed a problem after launch. The principles were real, and they had no contact with the work.

This is the gap I want to address. Responsible AI is not a statement of values. It is a set of practices that run inside the delivery process, with owners, tests, and consequences. Values that never touch a release are decoration. Here is how I think about turning them into something that ships.

A principle tells you what you care about. A practice tells you what you do on a Tuesday afternoon when a release is due and something looks off.

The difference matters because AI harm rarely comes from bad intentions. It comes from ordinary teams under ordinary deadline pressure, making reasonable-sounding choices without the information or the mandate to make a different one. A team does not decide to build an unfair system. It builds a system that works well on the data it tested, ships it on time, and never measures how it performs for the people who were underrepresented in that data.

Principles do not prevent that outcome, because principles do not run. Practices do. A required evaluation step, a named reviewer, a release checklist with items that can block, a dashboard that someone is accountable for reading. These are boring, and they are the only part of responsible AI that changes what actually reaches customers.

The useful test for any responsible AI programme is simple: show me a release that was delayed, changed, or stopped because of it. If nobody can, the programme is a communications exercise.

The most productive exercise I know is to take each principle and ask one question: what would we observe if we were violating it?

Fairness becomes "the error rate for any significant user group is not more than a defined margin worse than the overall rate." Transparency becomes "a user can tell, at the point of use, that an answer was generated and what it was based on." Privacy becomes "no personal data from one customer appears in output shown to another, and we test for it." Human oversight becomes "decisions above a defined impact threshold cannot complete without a named person approving them."

Each of those statements can be checked. Some can be automated and run on every change, like any other test. Some need a periodic review with evidence. Either way, they can fail, and when they fail, something happens.

This translation is uncomfortable, because it forces choices that principles let you avoid. What margin is acceptable? Which user groups count as significant? What is the impact threshold? Those are real decisions with real trade-offs, and they belong with accountable leaders, written down, rather than left implicit. A principle nobody has translated into a threshold is a principle nobody has agreed on.

Many organisations run their responsible AI review just before release. The feature is built, the launch date is set, marketing is ready, and a review group is asked to approve it. Under that arrangement the review can only do one of two things: wave it through, or become the reason the launch slipped. Teams quickly learn to see the review as an obstacle, and reviewers quickly learn that blocking is politically expensive.

The review that actually reduces harm happens at design time, when changing direction is cheap. Before much is built, the team writes down who the system affects, what decisions it influences, what the worst plausible failure looks like, and who bears the cost of that failure. They identify the groups most likely to be poorly served and plan how to measure performance for them. They decide which actions need a human and which can be automated.

This takes an hour or two for most features, and it changes what gets built. Design choices that would be impossible to reverse at launch, like which data to train or ground on, how much autonomy to grant, and whether to show confidence to the user, become simple to adjust. The launch-week review then becomes a check that the plan was followed, which is a much easier conversation.

The single most common way AI systems harm people quietly is through averages. A system can be ninety-five percent accurate overall and seventy percent accurate for a particular group, and the overall number will look excellent on every dashboard.

This happens for unremarkable reasons. The group is smaller in the data. Their language, documents, or circumstances differ from the majority. The test set was assembled from whatever was easy to collect. Nobody intended a gap, and nobody looked for one.

The practice is straightforward: decide in advance which segments matter for this system, measure quality separately for each of them, and set a threshold for the acceptable gap. Segments might be demographic, but often the most important ones are operational. New customers versus established ones. Non-native speakers. Unusual but legitimate cases. Customers in smaller markets. Documents in less common formats.

Then report the worst segment alongside the average, every time. Leaders get used to asking about the average. The responsible question is always "and who does it work worst for, and how badly?" If the team cannot answer, the system has not been evaluated responsibly, regardless of how good the headline number is.

Responsible AI fails most often not on knowledge but on authority. The concern is raised. Everyone agrees it is a concern. The release goes ahead anyway, because nobody had the clear right to stop it and the cost of delay was visible while the cost of harm was hypothetical.

Every AI system above a modest risk level needs a named person with the authority to block or pause it, and that authority has to be real. It should be written down, known to the delivery team, and backed by senior leadership when it is used. The person does not need to be a specialist ethicist. In most organisations it works best as part of an existing accountable role: the product owner for lower-risk systems, a risk or compliance lead for higher-risk ones.

Equally important, there must be a way for anyone on the team to raise a concern without career risk. Engineers and domain experts are often the first to notice that a system behaves badly for a particular group or in a particular situation. If raising that concern feels like being difficult, they will stop raising it, and you will learn about the problem from a customer, a journalist, or a regulator.

A practical signal of health: concerns are raised regularly, most are resolved without drama, and occasionally a release is held. A programme where nothing is ever raised is not a programme with no problems. It is a programme nobody trusts.

Two practices do more for user trust than almost anything else, and both are cheap to build.

The first is disclosure at the point of use. People should know when they are interacting with an AI system, when a decision about them was shaped by one, and roughly what it was based on. This does not mean a wall of legal text. It means a clear, plain statement in the interface, and where it matters, an indication of the sources or factors behind an answer.

The second is a route to contest. When an AI system makes or influences a decision that matters to someone, they need a way to say "this is wrong" and reach a human who can review it. That route needs to be visible, reasonably quick, and capable of actually changing the outcome. It also needs to feed back into the system. Every contested decision is evidence about where the system fails, and a well-run team reads those cases the way it reads production incidents.

Organisations sometimes resist both practices out of fear that they will draw attention to the system's limits. In practice the reverse happens. Users who can see what a system is doing and can challenge it when it is wrong trust it more, and they use it more.

The last shift is the one most programmes miss entirely. Responsible AI is usually treated as something you do before launch. But AI systems change after launch, sometimes without anyone touching them. User behaviour shifts. The data shifts. Upstream models are updated. A system that was fair and safe in its first month can drift into something else by its twelfth.

So the practices have to continue. Segment-level quality is monitored in production, not just measured once. Contested decisions are reviewed regularly for patterns. The design-time harm review is revisited when the system's scope, autonomy, or user base changes. Thresholds are rechecked against reality.

This has a cost, and that cost should be planned and budgeted rather than absorbed as a surprise. A useful rule of thumb is to treat responsible AI work as part of the system's ongoing operating cost, alongside hosting and support, rather than as a one-off compliance project.

The organisations that will earn lasting trust from customers, employees, and regulators are not the ones with the best-written principles. They are the ones that can show, for any AI system they run, how each principle was tested, who had the authority to stop it, how it performs for its worst-served users, and what happened the last time something went wrong. Principles describe what you value. Practices are the only proof that you meant it.

I write a field-note series on shipping AI that actually works in production. The original of this piece, and the rest, live on my LinkedIn. Originally published on LinkedIn.

Hire for Judgment, Not Prompts: How to Build an AI Team That Outlasts the Hype

📅 Nov 26, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Posted on Nov 26 • Originally published at linkedin.com

Every leadership team I talk to has the same line in its plan: "hire AI talent." It sits next to the budget for compute and the list of use cases, and it is usually the vaguest line on the page. Nobody can quite say who they are hiring, what that person will do in their first ninety days, or how anyone will know whether the hire worked.

So companies default to what they can see. They search for the newest job titles, screen for the newest vocabulary, and pay a premium for people who can talk fluently about the latest techniques. Twelve months later many of those teams have produced impressive demos and very little that runs in production, and the leader is asking why the expensive team did not deliver.

The answer is almost never that the people were not smart. It is that the company hired for the wrong scarce skill. What follows is how I think about building an AI team that still delivers after the hype cycle moves on.

The titles change every year. Prompt engineer, AI engineer, applied scientist, agent developer, AI product manager. The pattern underneath them does not change at all, because it is the same pattern every technology wave has produced.

When a new capability arrives, companies over-hire people who are fluent in the capability and under-hire people who know how to turn a capability into a dependable product. In the early web years it was people who could build a homepage versus people who could run a transaction system. In the early cloud years it was people who could spin up infrastructure versus people who could operate it at a sane cost. Fluency with the new thing is visible and easy to interview for. The ability to make it reliable, measurable, and safe is quieter and much harder to find.

AI makes this sharper than any wave before it, because the gap between a demo and a product is wider. A capable model can produce a convincing prototype in an afternoon. That prototype is perhaps a fifth of the work. The other four fifths are evaluation, data, integration, failure handling, cost control, and operation over time. A team built entirely from people who love the first fifth will keep producing first fifths.

Tool fluency has a short half-life. The specific techniques that were essential eighteen months ago are already partly automated or obsolete, and the ones that are essential today will follow. If your hiring bar is "knows the current toolkit," you are hiring for a skill that decays faster than your onboarding cycle.

What does not decay is judgment. Specifically, three kinds of it.

The first is judgment about whether an answer is good. AI systems produce output that looks right far more often than it is right. The people you need can look at a result and say, with reasons, whether it is correct, whether it is good enough for this use, and how they would prove it.

The second is judgment about where AI belongs. A surprising amount of value comes from people who can say "this part should be a rule, not a model" or "this step needs a human, not an agent." People who reach for AI everywhere create cost and risk you did not need.

The third is judgment about trade-offs. Speed against quality, cost against accuracy, autonomy against control. These are product and engineering decisions, and they require people who can hold several constraints at once and choose deliberately.

None of those skills is specific to AI. All of them are what separates a working AI product from an expensive experiment.

If I could make only one early hire on an AI team, it would not be the person who builds the system. It would be the person who can tell whether the system works.

This feels backwards to most leaders, because building is what produces visible progress. But a team that cannot measure quality has no way to know whether any change is an improvement. They tune prompts by feel, ship by enthusiasm, and discover problems from customers. Every week of building without evaluation is a week of work you cannot trust.

The evaluator role goes by different names, and sometimes it is a hat worn by a strong engineer rather than a separate job. What matters is the work: defining what correct means for each use case, building a representative test set, running it on every change, and reporting quality in numbers the business understands. The person doing this needs rigour, scepticism, and enough domain sense to know which errors matter.

Once that capability exists, everything else on the team gets faster. Builders can try ideas and get an answer in minutes rather than arguments in meetings. Leaders can approve releases on evidence. The evaluator is the hire that makes every other hire productive.

There is a persistent belief that AI work needs a different kind of person from ordinary software work. For research, perhaps. For building products, mostly not.

The engineers who succeed at shipping AI into production are, overwhelmingly, strong software engineers who have added AI to their toolkit. They write tests. They think about failure modes. They design for retries, timeouts, and partial failures. They care about logs, versioning, and the ability to roll back. They know that the model call is one component in a system, and that the system is what the user experiences.

The engineers who struggle are often the reverse: deeply fluent with models but uncomfortable with the plumbing that makes a product dependable. They can make the model do remarkable things in a notebook and cannot make it do ordinary things reliably at three in the morning.

So when you hire, weight the fundamentals heavily. A strong engineer can learn the current AI techniques in weeks, because those techniques are documented, discussed everywhere, and changing anyway. A person fluent in the techniques but weak on engineering discipline takes years to build the habits that keep production systems alive, if they ever do.

The most common structural mistake I see is treating domain experts as reviewers. The AI team builds something, then hands it to the people who understand the business (the claims handlers, the underwriters, the clinicians, the lawyers) for a sign-off at the end.

That arrangement guarantees rework. The domain expert finds problems the team could not have seen, the team goes back to rebuild, and everyone concludes that the experts are slowing things down.

The experts are not slowing things down. They are the only people who know what a correct answer looks like. In AI work, that knowledge is not a final check. It is the specification. It defines the test set, the edge cases, the acceptable error rate, and the difference between a harmless mistake and a dangerous one.

Put domain experts on the team from the first week, with real time allocated and real ownership of quality. Pay attention to the ones who are curious about the technology and sceptical of its output in equal measure. They are often your most valuable people, and they rarely appear in a search for "AI talent."

AI interviews have drifted towards vocabulary tests. Candidates are asked to explain techniques, list architectures, and discuss the latest models. The candidates who prepare best for these conversations are not necessarily the ones who will do the job best.

I prefer interviews that look like the work. Give a candidate a real, messy, anonymised task: a set of model outputs and a description of what the business needs, and ask them to decide which outputs are acceptable and why. Ask them how they would build a test for this use case and what they would do if quality dropped by ten points overnight. Show them a working prototype and ask what would worry them about putting it in front of customers.

These questions reveal judgment directly. Strong candidates ask about the users, the cost of errors, and how quality will be measured. Weaker candidates go straight to which model or technique they would use. Both kinds can sound impressive in a conventional interview. Only one kind will help you ship.

It also helps to ask every candidate about a time an AI system they built was wrong in production, and what they did. People who have run real systems have real answers. People who have only built demos tend to describe a demo.

The external market for experienced AI talent is expensive, competitive, and full of people with eighteen months of experience and a title that suggests five years. Some external hiring is necessary, especially for a few senior people who have taken AI products through a full lifecycle. But the most durable AI capability I have seen was mostly grown, not bought.

Your existing engineers already understand your systems, your data, and your constraints. Your existing domain experts already know what correct looks like. Giving them structured time, real projects, and a few experienced people to learn from often produces a stronger team than a hiring spree, at a fraction of the cost and with far less turnover.

This also changes the culture of adoption. When AI capability is built by people the organisation already trusts, the rest of the organisation trusts the output more. When it arrives as a separate, highly paid group with its own vocabulary, it is easy for everyone else to treat it as someone else's project.

A practical shape that works: hire two or three senior people who have shipped and operated AI in production, make evaluation and engineering discipline their first priority, pair them with your strongest existing engineers and domain experts, and measure the team on production outcomes rather than prototypes. Expand from there as the work proves itself.

The companies that will still have strong AI teams in five years are not the ones that won the bidding war for this year's titles. They are the ones that hired for judgment, built the capability to measure their own work, and grew people who understand both the technology and the business. That team does not go out of date when the tools change. It simply picks up the new tools and keeps shipping.

À propos de HopperChez Hopper, nous bâtissons la plateforme technologique de voyage de référence à l'échelle mondiale, et nous le faisons en résolvant de vrais problèmes pour de vrais voyageurs, partout sur la planète. Nos plateformes de réservation grand public Hopper et notre division B2B, HTS (Hopper Technology Solutions), travaillent en synergie pour offrir aux voyageurs transparence, flexibilité et de véritables économies à chaque séjour. Pour y parvenir, nous combinons d'immenses volumes de données et l'intelligence artificielle à des produits fintech exclusifs. Nous ne sommes pas simplement un moteur de réservation de plus : nous offrons une façon fondamentalement meilleure de planifier et de vivre le voyage pour nos clients et nos partenaires. Nous sommes la preuve que ce qui est avantageux pour le client l'est tout autant pour l'entreprise.

Et notre croissance s'accélère! L’application Hopper a été téléchargée plus de 120 millions de fois, et 70 % de nos utilisateurs appartiennent à la génération Z et aux millénariaux — les voyageurs de demain. Aujourd'hui, notre plus grand levier consiste à propulser les solutions de fintech de voyage, de commerce et de fidélisation pour les plus grandes marques de l’industrie. Notre premier partenariat HTS avec Capital One a permis de lancer un portail de voyage dédié aux titulaires de cartes de cette grande marque financière. Depuis, nous nous sommes associés aux plus grands noms du voyage et du secteur bancaire, notamment Air Canada, Uber, la Banque Royale du Canada (RBC) et Nubank, en alimentant aussi bien une simple intégration fintech ciblée qu'un portail complet de fidélisation voyage clé en main.

Voilà notre trajectoire : nous avons fait nos débuts comme une petite application novatrice dans l'univers du voyage, et nous sommes désormais le moteur sous le capot qui propulse la technologie du voyage mondial.

Des milliards de dollars en voyages et en solutions fintech transitent chaque année par Hopper et HTS

Nos produits fintech, dont l'annulation sans motif (Cancel for Any Reason) et l'assistance en cas de perturbation (Disruption Assistance for Any Reason), affichent des taux de satisfaction client exceptionnels grâce à des conditions limpides et des résolutions instantanées, sans poser de questions

Près de 30 % des clients de l'application ajoutent un produit fintech à leur réservation, et ces clients sont 1,6 fois plus susceptibles de réserver à nouveau avec nous

HTS génère désormais plus de 90 % des activités de l'entreprise, démontrant la rapidité avec laquelle notre volet B2B s'est développé à grande échelle

Grâce à HTS, n'importe quel fournisseur de voyages (transporteurs aériens, hôtels, banques, agences de voyages) peut intégrer les solutions fintech, commerciales et d'IA de Hopper directement dans ses propres canaux, qu'il s'agisse d'une intégration spécifique ou d'un portail de voyage complet de bout en bout

About the RoleHTS (Hopper Technology Solutions) is Hopper’s B2B division, powering travel AI solutions across leading airlines, hotels and financial institutions globally. The Marketing & Communications team is looking for a Senior B2B Performance Marketing Manager to lead growth marketing for its B2B business across digital channels. The team is lean and senior, ownership is broad, and the expectation is that the candidate handles both strategy and execution.

Own the B2B digital marketing strategy for HTS, setting channel priorities, budgets, and targets tied to pipeline and revenue

Plan, launch, and optimize paid campaigns across LinkedIn, Google Ads, and other digital channels, from audience and creative through to reporting

Build and run lead generation programs end to end, working with Sales to define lead quality and keep improving it

Develop content for digital campaigns, including social content, search ads, and more

A/B test content and ad formats to optimize for lead generation and conversion

Test and scale new channels and tactics, and know when to cut what isn’t working

Track, analyze, and report on performance, including cost per lead, conversion rates, and pipeline contribution, and turn the data into clear recommendations for the team

Partner with Product, Sales, Legal, and Communications to keep messaging consistent and campaigns aligned with business priorities

Drive quality over quantity, optimizing campaigns for sales-qualified leads (SQLs) rather than raw lead volume, and working with Sales to continuously refine targeting, messaging, and lead criteria so that marketing effort translates into real pipeline

Work closely with the Marketing & Communications team while operating with a high degree of independence

Report on digital performance to senior leadership, translating channel metrics like cost per lead, conversion rates, and pipeline contribution into clear insights and recommendations that inform marketing investment and strategy

Work with sales, leadership and marketing comms to create strategy and process for tracking marketing leads through the entire sales pipeline

Provide comprehensive insights on how marketing campaigns influenced pipeline progression and revenue

Potential to support growth within existing partners over time, through expansion campaigns and joint product launches with partner teams and Comms

Comfort working at both levels: you can set the strategy and also build, launch, manage, optimize, and report on the campaigns yourself

Strong analytical skills and fluency in reporting tools, CRM, and marketing automation platforms

A self-starter mindset, with the ability to prioritize, manage your own workload, and deliver without close oversight

Excellent written and verbal communication skills, and the ability to collaborate across teams and with senior stakeholders

Experience in tech, travel, or B2B environments is a strong asset

Comfort in a lean, senior team where ownership is broad and no task is beneath you

Well-funded and proven startup with large ambitions, competitive salary and upsides of pre-IPO equity packages

About HopperAt Hopper, we're building the leading travel technology platform in the world, and we're doing it by solving real problems for real travelers globally. Our Hopper consumer booking platforms and HTS (Hopper Technology Solutions), our B2B business, work together to give travelers something the industry has never reliably offered: transparency, flexibility, and real savings on every trip. We combine massive amounts of data and AI with proprietary fintech products to make that happen, not just another booking engine, but a fundamentally better way to plan and experience travel for our customers and our partners. We are proof that better-for-the-customer and better-for-the-business can be one in the same.

That's our trajectory: we started as a small, disruptive app within the travel space, and now we're the engine under the hood powering how Travel Tech works.

The opt-in, AI-assisted checks: vision, SEO, brand voice, and semantic matching

📅 Nov 26, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Part 6 of 6 in CatalogSentry's launch series.

Part 5 closed out the deterministic checks. This post covers the 7 checks that are off by default, each calling this Actor's own operator-hosted AI backend — no API key or endpoint for you to configure, just enable them in checks. Six use AI-assisted detection directly; the seventh, semantic_cannibalization, is deterministic by default with an optional AI-assisted pass layered on top. Six of the seven examples below are real findings from the 995-product Flipkart run; one (translation_consistency) is constructed, for a reason explained in its own section.

Worth repeating from part 2: these checks involve model judgment, not a fact lookup. The evidence is grounded in something real (the image, the text), but the check is asserting "a model looked at this and concluded X," not "this is objectively true." Every finding below says so explicitly in its own explanation field.

Looks at the product image, lists concrete attributes actually visible in it, and flags whichever ones aren't mentioned anywhere in the title or description.

Suggests keywords grounded in the image or existing text that the listing doesn't currently use — a discoverability gap, not an invented claim about the product.

Needs brandStyleBrief set — a short description of your expected product photo style (e.g. "single item, centered, white background"). No brief, no findings; this check never guesses what your brand standard is. From the real run (brief: single centered product shot):

Needs categoryVoiceBriefs — a map of category name to a tone/positioning brief. Only categories with a brief set get checked; everything else is skipped, no cost.

Covered briefly in part 4 — embeds title+description and flags pairs above a similarity threshold, catching duplicates that exact-match checks can't see because nothing about the text literally matches.

A similarity of 1.000 here isn't a rounding fluke — it means the two listings' text is effectively identical to the embedding model, even though they're filed as separate SKUs with no shared GTIN.

The one check in this list that's deterministic by default: a word-overlap (Jaccard) pass over every pair of product descriptions, catching two differently titled listings whose body copy is near-identical — they end up competing for the same search intent instead of each serving a clear purpose. An optional AI embedding pass can be layered on top to also catch paraphrased (not just overlapping) descriptions; it's the one check whose cost scales with the square of catalog size, so it has its own budget control (maxEstimatedCostUsd) rather than the simpler per-product limit the vision checks use.

Two completely different product names — a shampoo combo and a "Euro Style Combo Set" — sharing two-thirds of their description's vocabulary. Neither duplicate_detection (no shared GTIN, no matching title) nor a human skimming the title column would catch this.

This check needs targetLanguages set — it wasn't configured for the 995-product Flipkart run, so the check didn't fire, not because it found nothing but because it was never asked to run at all (no candidates, same as any check with an unmet precondition). So unlike every other finding in this series, what follows is a constructed example of the check's deterministic core, run through the actual extraction function this repo already uses for title_description_contradiction — not the full check (which also needs a live AI call to generate the translation itself):

That's the actual mismatch logic: the same regex-based number extraction title_description_contradiction uses, applied to an AI-generated translation instead of a second feed field. If an AI translation of "256GB" becomes "128GB" in another language, this is how CatalogSentry would catch that specific, narrow failure mode — a number that must stay identical regardless of language, but didn't. It does not check whether the rest of the translation reads naturally; that's out of scope by design (see the module's own docstring in the repo).

15 checks, 8 deterministic and on by default, 7 opt-in — every one of them demonstrated with either real output from a real feed, or an explicit, labeled exception. If you've read all six parts: this is the complete, current state of what CatalogSentry checks, with nothing described that isn't actually shipped.

Want to see all 15 run end-to-end on a real feed? Try the interactive demo, or run it directly on Apify Store — it's live today.
